title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox:Better Models from Worse Perturbations

paper.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
paper.abstract: Abstract How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Optimization using population-based search, i.e. evolutionary computation, relies on generating and selecting high-quality candidates. Genetic algorithms optimize by discovering beneficial recombinations and mutations along with selection of candidates with higher fitness ( Goldberg, 1989 ) . Particle swarm optimization pressures particles to search for better positions while maintaining the previously best found positions ( Eberhart & Kennedy, 1995 ) . The original evolution strategies (ES) compared a single parent to a single offspring and selected the better solution ( Rechenberg, 1965 ) . In each of these methods, the generation of higher-fitness candidate solutions is crucial to the optimization process. For ES specifically, this story has changed over time. With the introduction of natural evolution strategies ( Wierstra et al., 2011 , NES,) , which updates the parent model using a weighted sum of all generated candidates, ES was shown to potentially behave as a gradient approximator instead of working through the selection of candidates with an improved fitness. NES was a precursor to implementation of ES on large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) problems such as Atari ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) that then inspired theoretical analysis that found that ES with isotropic Gaussian noise is a gradient estimate: with high enough population sizes (ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands), correlation between the ES update direction and network gradient stays consistent while ES performance on a per-iteration basis would match that of backpropagation ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) . This along with further work concluded that ES operated as a gradient estimator that naturally favors robustness ( Lehman et al., 2018 ) . Figure 1: The Evolution Strategies Paradox across three examples: OLMo 2 7B fine-tuned on Sudoku, Qwen 2.5 7B fine-tuned on Countdown, and a 60K parameter CNN on MNIST. Left plots show the fraction of offspring models better than the parent model; right plots show the training curves (i.e. the performance of the parent models over time). In each case, offspring models perform worse than the parent model for nearly all of training, while the parent models consistently improve. Recently, a new opportunity for ES has emerged: scaling to the vastly larger optimization problem of fine-tuning Large Language Models ( Qiu et al., 2026 , LLMs;) . This work shifted from centered rank rewards to z-score normalized rewards, but more surprisingly, it brought the population size down from thousands to just 30 ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Hayes et al., 2026 ) . With such small populations in a space of billions of parameters, accurate gradient estimation appears infeasible. It was further demonstrated that large pretrained models have a rich search landscape with many directions for improvement ( Liang et al., 2026 ; Gan & Isola, 2026 ) . (a) Visual representation of ES Paradox (b) Fraction of population members outperforming parent at various batch sizes. Figure 2: Tracking the ES paradox: (a) A visual representation of the ES paradox over iterations in a training run. At each iteration, offspring are generated which are all worse than the parent model in measured reward. (b) Fraction of perturbations better than the parent in the Sudoku fine-tuning task over iterations in the training run. Larger batch size leads to less noise in the reward landscape, and makes the paradox more prominent. Taken together, these results suggest that in LLM-scale spaces, ES is not based on gradient estimation, but relies on finding good candidates among sampled perturbations and moving towards them, as other evolutionary methods do. However, the results in this paper contradict that hypothesis as well: ES is found to make consistent progress even when all offspring candidates are worse than the parent (Figure 1 ). This paradox is observed across a range of ES optimization tasks, suggesting that it is a general property of high-dimensional ES optimization. While it had been hypothesized possible for individual steps with alternative forms of ES under idealized conditions ( Ba et al., 2026 ) , this work is the first empirical demonstration of this occurring. A further analysis reveals that this phenomenon results from three mechanisms (1) Consistent curvature of the search landscape results in decreased performance with increased perturbation size; (2) relative performance between offspring still differentiates good and bad directions in parameter space; and (3) the ES preserves the signal of good directions while reducing noise in the aggregated update (Figure 2 ). The remainder of the paper is as follows: Section 2 details the ES update and the experimental setup in LLM fine-tuning under which the paradox is observed. The next three sections then focus on each of the three mechanisms. Section 3 runs a landscape analysis, finding that increased perturbation size is strongly tied to a decrease in reward. Section 4 demonstrates that even at larger perturbations where all offspring are worse than the parent, good directions can still be identified. Section 5 uses an analytical model of ES to show that the updates aggregate those good directions while reducing noise, making the paradox likely. These findings thus demonstrate a previously unknown mechanism, indeed a paradigm shift in optimization, that allows scaling perturbation-based optimization to modern LLMs.

sections.heading: 2 The Evolution Strategies Paradox
sections.text: This work uses ES as implemented by Qiu et al. (2026) , which is characterized by isotropic Gaussian perturbations, low population size, and z-score normalized rewards. For each ES iteration t t , let a parent model be parameterized by current parameters θ t ∈ ℝ d \theta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . A set of N N perturbation vectors, indexed i ∈ { 1 , 2 , … ​ N } i\in\{1,2,...N\} is drawn from isotropic gaussian noise, ϵ i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) . Each perturbation is then multiplied by perturbation scale σ ∈ ℝ + \sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{+} , and added to θ t \theta_{t} to create a population of offspring models , parameterized by θ t + σ ​ ϵ i \theta_{t}+\sigma\epsilon_{i} . Each offspring model is evaluated to obtain a reward R i R_{i} , and the ES update is then the average of the perturbations, weighted by the z-score of the model rewards: Δ ​ θ = θ t + 1 − θ t = α N ​ ∑ i = 1 N Z i ​ ϵ i , Z i = R i − μ R σ R , \Delta\theta\;=\;\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\;=\;\frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\,\epsilon_{i},\qquad Z_{i}\;=\;\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}}, (1) where α \alpha is the step size, μ R \mu_{R} and σ R \sigma_{R} are the mean and standard deviation of this population’s rewards, and weights Z i Z_{i} are the z-score normalized rewards. These updates are iterated until a stopping criterion, as shown in the basic ES training Algorithm 1 . For an iteration t t , let A t A_{t} denote the event that all offspring at iteration t t perform worse than their parent. The ES paradox occurs when the update still improves the parent model in expectation under this event: A t = { R ( θ t + σ ϵ i ) < R ( θ t ) ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , N } } , 𝔼 [ R ( θ t + 1 ) − R ( θ t ) | A t ] > 0 . A_{t}=\Big\{R\big(\theta_{t}+\sigma\epsilon_{i}\big)<R(\theta_{t})\;\;\forall\,i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\Big\},\qquad\mathbb{E}\big[\,R(\theta_{t+1})-R(\theta_{t})\,\big|\,A_{t}\,\big]>0. (2) In training runs, the paradox is tracked by recording the fraction of perturbations with rewards better than the current parent on the training reward. When this metric stays at or close to zero for extended periods of time while reward increases, it is assumed the paradox is occurring. In this paper, the performance on training data is treated as the full reward landscape; however, the effect can still occur when measured with a held-out reward. Monitoring this parent reward adds a marginal inference cost to ES training runs, as one additional model evaluation must be run for each sampled population. Figure 1 displays this metric alongside training progress in fine-tuning in the three example tasks. Each training run starts with significant fractions of perturbations outperforming the parent model, but partway into training, this metric falls to zero. The effect is most prominent with a fixed batch, though it can occur in shuffled batches; all else equal larger batch sizes make the effect stronger, as shown in Figure 2 . This paper’s analysis focuses on LLM fine-tuning tasks, where it was first discovered. Two examples of the paradox in LLM fine-tuning are more carefully analyzed: a 500-iteration training run on a 4 × 4 4\times 4 Sudoku task, and a 500-iteration training run on a countdown task ( Pan et al., 2025 ) , using harnesses and grading used in Zhao et al. (2025) . In both these examples, Qwen 2.5 7B-Instruct was used as the LLM, evaluated at temperature zero; ES was run with hyperparameters (N = 30, σ \sigma = 0.001, α \alpha = 5 × 10 -4 ). Fine-tuning was done with a dataset of 800 problems, with the batch size set to the entire dataset to demonstrate a strong effect (Figure 2 ). Although the analysis focused on Qwen 2.5 with these two specific tasks, the paradox has been observed in other models as well, such as OLMo 2 7B, as shown in Figure 1 . In addition to LLM fine-tuning, the ES paradox occurs in other domains of ES optimization of neural networks. One such domain is included in this paper: training of a randomly initialized 60,000-parameter Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on MNIST. The paradox was reproduced with ES parameters N = 16, σ \sigma = 0.04, and α \alpha = 0.02. Thus, the paradox can be seen as a general phenomenon across models, tasks, and modalities. The next three sections analyze the mechanisms that produce it and demonstrate that it is a side effect of effective optimization in high-dimensional search spaces. sections.heading: 3 Why Are Offspring Worse Than the Parent?
sections.text: As a first step to understand how the ES paradox emerges, this section examines the relationship between perturbation size and reward in fine-tuning tasks. For both Sudoku and Countdown fine-tuning tasks, checkpoints from every 100 iterations were taken, and 300 offspring were generated at varying perturbation magnitudes. These perturbed models were then evaluated on the original fixed training set of 800 problems, producing a distribution of model rewards at each magnitude. The magnitudes were chosen to match the average magnitude of perturbations with σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} and σ \sigma from 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} in steps of 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} . Figure 3 displays these tests at the base model and at iterations 100 and 500 in the training run, with box-and-whisker plots displayed at each perturbation magnitude. With the base model, the mean reward is largely constant, but its variation increases approximately linearly as perturbation size increases. By iteration 100, perturbation magnitude has a significant, consistent, negative effect on the reward. By iteration 500, this effect is even more consistent and pronounced. In Sudoku in particular, the rewards at magnitude matching the σ \sigma used for training (1e-3) are multiple standard deviations below those of the parent model. Therefore, the perturbation reward distribution strongly depends on the perturbation size ( σ \sigma ). Small σ \sigma ’s produce valid offspring for model improvement, whereas large σ \sigma nearly guarantees that no better models will be produced. If large σ \sigma values in the range where the paradox occurs (e.g. σ = 10 − 3 \sigma=10^{-3} ) lead to worse performance, why not use σ \sigma in the range of ( 1.0 × 10 − 4 , 2.5 × 10 − 4 ) (1.0\times 10^{-4},2.5\times 10^{-4}) where improvement is possible? Indeed, in Figure 3 , when σ \sigma is small enough, the distribution sometimes exceeds parent performance, suggesting that opportunities for improvement exist. However, when σ \sigma is set to these values, ES progress is significantly less, as is tested and shown in Figure 4 . The improvements are lost in the noise, as discussed in detail in Section 5 . However, even though large σ \sigma values result in degraded performance, it turns out they can be used to identify good directions reliably, as discussed in the next section. Checkpoints in Countdown and Sudoku training runs were perturbed 300 times at each specified magnitude, and distributions of rewards were plotted. As the magnitudes increase, the means decrease, and the variance increases. Thus, the offspring are likely to perform worse than the parent. (a) Fine-tuning performance on Sudoku (b) Fraction of offspring that outperform parent. Even though the smaller perturbation magnitudes produce better candidates, the larger perturbations produce better directions and thus a better overall training run.

sections.heading: 4 How Are Good Directions Identified?
sections.text: Section 3 leads to the question: When all models perform worse than the current model, does their relative performance still indicate which directions are more promising? Although it is not possible to directly measure the reward gradient for model checkpoints, it is possible to evaluate the relative performance of perturbations across magnitudes where improving directions do and do not occur. If significant correlations are seen across magnitudes, regardless of performance, then relative performance is indicative of good directions regardless of all perturbation offspring performing worse than the parent. To test this hypothesis, the checkpoints from Sudoku and Countdown runs were again used. The set of 300 perturbation directions was evaluated on each task’s respective 800-problem dataset at magnitudes corresponding to σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} and σ \sigma from 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} in steps of 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} . A correlation matrix was then constructed between the relative rewards of perturbations at these magnitudes. If the perturbation rewards at large σ \sigma contain a signal, then they should correlate with the rewards of the same perturbations at small σ \sigma . From Figure 5 we can see indeed, the rewards are significantly correlated between large and small perturbations, even when the rewards of large perturbations are significantly lower than those of the small perturbations. While greater magnitude differences reduce the measured correlation, the correlations remain positive in most cases. These correlations likely emerge due to a special property of ES with isotropic Gaussian noise in high-dimensional settings. This noise occupies a thin shell in what has been referred to as a “soap bubble” effect ( Huszár, 2017 ) . In a high-dimensional space, all perturbations are nearly identical in norm, effectively canceling out any isotropic curvature in the reward landscape, while leaving differences in relative performance due to the gradient. In other words, the magnitude of noise is identical in all directions, and thus, relative performance allows a signal to still emerge. One way to take advantage of the good directions at large σ \sigma would be to simply follow the best perturbation, instead of performing the aggregation through a weighted sum. To evaluate this ablation, a second test was implemented. The perturbation rewards were sampled on the standard (large) σ \sigma (1e-3), the best of them identified, and the perturbation was scaled down to the size of an average ES update (i.e. a small σ \sigma ). A 500-iteration training run was then run with this process. The training curves along with the fraction of perturbations better than the parent are displayed in Figure 6 . While this best-of-N selection allows making progress, it is still outperformed by the actual ES update. This result suggests that an additional mechanism of aggregation contributes further to the ES performance, as will be discussed next. Figure 5: Correlation between rewards at various perturbation magnitudes σ \sigma at iterations 200 and 500 iterations in the Sudoku Fine-Tuning task. The σ \sigma range at which the paradox occurs, i.e. the best of the 30 offspring has a lower reward than the parent, is labeled with red arrows. The rewards at small and large σ \sigma correlate significantly. Thus, the same good directions can be identified at various perturbation magnitudes, even at which all the perturbations are worse than the parent. (a) Training performance of scaled best-of-30 perturbation selection compared with the actual aggregated ES update. (b) Fraction of the perturbations with the best-of-30 method that outperform the parent. Figure 6: Best-of-30 selection ablation: (a) Training performance of scaled best-of-30 perturbation selection compared with the actual aggregated ES update. (b) Fraction of the perturbations with the best-of-30 method that are better than the parent. When scaled from a size where the best perturbation performs worse to the size of a typical ES update, the model is able to improve. However, the aggregated ES update direction still significantly outperforms this best-of-30 direction, suggesting that aggregation contributes further to performance.

sections.heading: 5 How Do the Updates Improve Performance?
sections.text: Sections 3 and 4 demonstrated that model performance decreases with increasing perturbation; however, even when all offspring are worse than the parent, good search directions can be identified among them. This section demonstrates how the ES aggregation mechanism adds value. The insights are drawn from an analytical model of the ES update in a reward landscape with observation noise and quadratic loss. In this model, the ES update can be decomposed into a signal component along the gradient and a noise component orthogonal to it. The model shows that, in expectation, the ES update moves a fixed distance in the direction of the signal, while reducing the magnitude of the noise component via aggregation of offspring. The mean and variance of the ES update in this model were derived independently by ( Hoy et al., 2026 ) , along with a similar decomposition of signal and noise of the update, which they use to estimate parameter drift over training runs. The analysis here differs by focusing on the per-step reward improvement and its relationship to observation noise and curvature. In the subsections below, the update decomposition is first defined in a simplified linear reward landscape. A realistic observation noise term is then introduced, and the model is extended to include curvature. In the end, the optimal perturbation magnitude is determined in the model, showing that it results in likely improvements. All along, these results are validated empirically with existing training runs.

The reward of these updates was measured, and confidence intervals drawn for the mean reward update (Figure 8 ). Notice that, as predicted by the noise-curvature model, the expected reward update increases and then plateaus with population size. Further, the update sizes are highly consistent, and even as their magnitude decreases significantly with respect to population size, the reward improvement remains the same. This result demonstrates that the ES update is holding the signal constant while reducing noise. These plots also illuminate why ES is able to work on billion-parameter models with population sizes of only 30: once the noise is reduced enough to avoid the curvature penalty, ES achieves its maximum possible improvement on each step. sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Future Work
sections.text: The ES paradox emerged as an unexpected anomaly in population-based search in large spaces. Such methods are presumed to work by creating offspring that are better than parents, yet in many cases ES is able to consistently improve even when this is not true. Understanding the mechanisms behind this paradox led to a new way of thinking about search in high-dimensional spaces: instead of an anomaly, the paradox is a side effect of a principled interaction of noise and curvature in such spaces. This mechanism is different from gradient descent, simulated annealing, and other evolutionary computation, so much so that it can be seen as a paradigm shift in the sense of Kuhn (1970) : an anomaly becomes a fundamental principle in the new way of seeing things. As a result, old assumptions need to be re-evaluated, and new opportunities arise for progress. For instance:

sections.heading: Small Population Performance of ES:
sections.text: One of the most dramatic features of the new line of ES work in LLM fine-tuning has been the significantly smaller population size. Previously, it had been assumed that ES had fundamental scaling limitations with respect to high-dimensional spaces ( Jamieson et al., 2012 ) , yet within fine-tuning, it has been competitive with, and often even outperforming, gradient-based reinforcement learning methods. This work now sheds some light on this phenomenon, demonstrating that once the noise component of the ES update is small enough to avoid incurring a significant cost from curvature, the update is able to achieve the maximum improvement in reward - even if the noise component is orders of magnitude larger than the signal component.

sections.heading: The surprising Robustness of LLMs to Noise in Parameter Space:
sections.text: From the update reward improvement estimate results in Figure 8 , per step update is seen to plateau at approximately a population size of 30. Given the analysis in Section 5 , this would imply each ES update contains a signal component of maximum magnitude α \alpha , while the noise component contains a magnitude of α ​ d − 1 N = α ​ 7 × 10 9 30 ≈ α × 15,000 \alpha\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{N}}=\alpha\sqrt{\frac{7\times 10^{9}}{30}}\approx\alpha\times 15,000 . While fine-tuning, for every unit distance ES moves the network in the direction of model improvement, it moves 15,000 unit distances in an irrelevant direction. This is consistent with ( Hoy et al., 2026 ) which finds that the total parameter drift of ES-fine-tuned LLMs follows the random-walk prediction α 2 ​ T ​ d / N \alpha^{2}Td/N to within a few percent. This demonstrates a surprising fact that LLMs can have their parameters dramatically modified in random directions without affecting performance.

sections.heading: Future Work:
sections.text: Results and the analytical model suggest that there may be ways to further optimize the hyperparameters of ES. Section 5.4 presented an optimal perturbation size conditional on observation noise and curvature. Future work may look at how to identify these properties during a run, or whether estimation of said optimums is too noisy to do online, but may be aggregated across fine-tuning runs. Additional work could also modify the ES algorithm itself to take advantage of this new paradigm, where improving offspring is no longer necessary for population-based optimization.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The ES paradox presents a counterintuitive conclusion: that ES can learn while consistently generating worse offspring than its parent. This paper demonstrates why this is possible: even when all offspring perform worse than their parent, their relative performance contains valuable information for improving directions. The ES update then aggregates this signal while reducing the noise to a point where improvement can be made. Together, these results suggest that ES in large-dimensional spaces can be seen as a new optimization paradigm: it takes advantage of the interactions of noise and curvature in such spaces the way other standard methods do not. The results provide insight into how ES is able to function effectively on billion-parameter LLMs, and suggest opportunities for improving the method further.

Hayes, Elliot Meyerson, Babak Hodjat, Risto Miikkulainen, Xin Qiu † † thanks: Corresponding author: roberto.dailey@cognizant.com Affiliation: Cognizant AI Lab, San Francisco Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin Abstract How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general. 1 Introduction Optimization using population-based search, i.e. evolutionary computation, relies on generating and selecting high-quality candidates. Genetic algorithms optimize by discovering beneficial recombinations and mutations along with selection of candidates with higher fitness ( Goldberg, 1989 ) . Particle swarm optimization pressures particles to search for better positions while maintaining the previously best found positions ( Eberhart & Kennedy, 1995 ) . The original evolution strategies (ES) compared a single parent to a single offspring and selected the better solution ( Rechenberg, 1965 ) . In each of these methods, the generation of higher-fitness candidate solutions is crucial to the optimization process. For ES specifically, this story has changed over time. With the introduction of natural evolution strategies ( Wierstra et al., 2011 , NES,) , which updates the parent model using a weighted sum of all generated candidates, ES was shown to potentially behave as a gradient approximator instead of working through the selection of candidates with an improved fitness. NES was a precursor to implementation of ES on large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) problems such as Atari ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) that then inspired theoretical analysis that found that ES with isotropic Gaussian noise is a gradient estimate: with high enough population sizes (ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands), correlation between the ES update direction and network gradient stays consistent while ES performance on a per-iteration basis would match that of backpropagation ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) . This along with further work concluded that ES operated as a gradient estimator that naturally favors robustness ( Lehman et al., 2018 ) . Figure 1: The Evolution Strategies Paradox across three examples: OLMo 2 7B fine-tuned on Sudoku, Qwen 2.5 7B fine-tuned on Countdown, and a 60K parameter CNN on MNIST. Left plots show the fraction of offspring models better than the parent model; right plots show the training curves (i.e. the performance of the parent models over time). In each case, offspring models perform worse than the parent model for nearly all of training, while the parent models consistently improve. Recently, a new opportunity for ES has emerged: scaling to the vastly larger optimization problem of fine-tuning Large Language Models ( Qiu et al., 2026 , LLMs;) . This work shifted from centered rank rewards to z-score normalized rewards, but more surprisingly, it brought the population size down from thousands to just 30 ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Hayes et al., 2026 ) . With such small populations in a space of billions of parameters, accurate gradient estimation appears infeasible. It was further demonstrated that large pretrained models have a rich search landscape with many directions for improvement ( Liang et al., 2026 ; Gan & Isola, 2026 ) . At each iteration, offspring are generated which are all worse than the parent model in measured reward. (b) Fraction of perturbations better than the parent in the Sudoku fine-tuning task over iterations in the training run. Larger batch size leads to less noise in the reward landscape, and makes the paradox more prominent. Taken together, these results suggest that in LLM-scale spaces, ES is not based on gradient estimation, but relies on finding good candidates among sampled perturbations and moving towards them, as other evolutionary methods do. However, the results in this paper contradict that hypothesis as well: ES is found to make consistent progress even when all offspring candidates are worse than the parent (Figure 1 ). This paradox is observed across a range of ES optimization tasks, suggesting that it is a general property of high-dimensional ES optimization. While it had been hypothesized possible for individual steps with alternative forms of ES under idealized conditions ( Ba et al., 2026 ) , this work is the first empirical demonstration of this occurring. A further analysis reveals that this phenomenon results from three mechanisms (1) Consistent curvature of the search landscape results in decreased performance with increased perturbation size; (2) relative performance between offspring still differentiates good and bad directions in parameter space; and (3) the ES preserves the signal of good directions while reducing noise in the aggregated update (Figure 2 ). The remainder of the paper is as follows: Section 2 details the ES update and the experimental setup in LLM fine-tuning under which the paradox is observed. The next three sections then focus on each of the three mechanisms. Section 3 runs a landscape analysis, finding that increased perturbation size is strongly tied to a decrease in reward. Section 4 demonstrates that even at larger perturbations where all offspring are worse than the parent, good directions can still be identified. Section 5 uses an analytical model of ES to show that the updates aggregate those good directions while reducing noise, making the paradox likely. These findings thus demonstrate a previously unknown mechanism, indeed a paradigm shift in optimization, that allows scaling perturbation-based optimization to modern LLMs. 2 The Evolution Strategies Paradox This work uses ES as implemented by Qiu et al. (2026) , which is characterized by isotropic Gaussian perturbations, low population size, and z-score normalized rewards. For each ES iteration t t , let a parent model be parameterized by current parameters θ t ∈ ℝ d \theta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . A set of N N perturbation vectors, indexed i ∈ { 1 , 2 , … ​ N } i\in\{1,2,...N\} is drawn from isotropic gaussian noise, ϵ i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) . Each perturbation is then multiplied by perturbation scale σ ∈ ℝ + \sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{+} , and added to θ t \theta_{t} to create a population of offspring models , parameterized by θ t + σ ​ ϵ i \theta_{t}+\sigma\epsilon_{i} . Each offspring model is evaluated to obtain a reward R i R_{i} , and the ES update is then the average of the perturbations, weighted by the z-score of the model rewards: Δ ​ θ = θ t + 1 − θ t = α N ​ ∑ i = 1 N Z i ​ ϵ i , Z i = R i − μ R σ R , \Delta\theta\;=\;\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\;=\;\frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\,\epsilon_{i},\qquad Z_{i}\;=\;\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}}, (1) where α \alpha is the step size, μ R \mu_{R} and σ R \sigma_{R} are the mean and standard deviation of this population’s rewards, and weights Z i Z_{i} are the z-score normalized rewards. These updates are iterated until a stopping criterion, as shown in the basic ES training Algorithm 1 . For an iteration t t , let A t A_{t} denote the event that all offspring at iteration t t perform worse than their parent. The ES paradox occurs when the update still improves the parent model in expectation under this event: A t = { R ( θ t + σ ϵ i ) < R ( θ t ) ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , N } } , 𝔼 [ R ( θ t + 1 ) − R ( θ t ) | A t ] > 0 . (2) In training runs, the paradox is tracked by recording the fraction of perturbations with rewards better than the current parent on the training reward. When this metric stays at or close to zero for extended periods of time while reward increases, it is assumed the paradox is occurring. In this paper, the performance on training data is treated as the full reward landscape; however, the effect can still occur when measured with a held-out reward. Monitoring this parent reward adds a marginal inference cost to ES training runs, as one additional model evaluation must be run for each sampled population. Figure 1 displays this metric alongside training progress in fine-tuning in the three example tasks. Each training run starts with significant fractions of perturbations outperforming the parent model, but partway into training, this metric falls to zero. The effect is most prominent with a fixed batch, though it can occur in shuffled batches; all else equal larger batch sizes make the effect stronger, as shown in Figure 2 . This paper’s analysis focuses on LLM fine-tuning tasks, where it was first discovered. Two examples of the paradox in LLM fine-tuning are more carefully analyzed: a 500-iteration training run on a 4 × 4 4\times 4 Sudoku task, and a 500-iteration training run on a countdown task ( Pan et al., 2025 ) , using harnesses and grading used in Zhao et al. (2025) . In both these examples, Qwen 2.5 7B-Instruct was used as the LLM, evaluated at temperature zero; ES was run with hyperparameters (N = 30, σ \sigma = 0.001, α \alpha = 5 × 10 -4 ). Fine-tuning was done with a dataset of 800 problems, with the batch size set to the entire dataset to demonstrate a strong effect (Figure 2 ). Although the analysis focused on Qwen 2.5 with these two specific tasks, the paradox has been observed in other models as well, such as OLMo 2 7B, as shown in Figure 1 . In addition to LLM fine-tuning, the ES paradox occurs in other domains of ES optimization of neural networks. One such domain is included in this paper: training of a randomly initialized 60,000-parameter Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on MNIST. The paradox was reproduced with ES parameters N = 16, σ \sigma = 0.04, and α \alpha = 0.02. Thus, the paradox can be seen as a general phenomenon across models, tasks, and modalities. The next three sections analyze the mechanisms that produce it and demonstrate that it is a side effect of effective optimization in high-dimensional search spaces. As a first step to understand how the ES paradox emerges, this section examines the relationship between perturbation size and reward in fine-tuning tasks. For both Sudoku and Countdown fine-tuning tasks, checkpoints from every 100 iterations were taken, and 300 offspring were generated at varying perturbation magnitudes. These perturbed models were then evaluated on the original fixed training set of 800 problems, producing a distribution of model rewards at each magnitude. The magnitudes were chosen to match the average magnitude of perturbations with σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} and σ \sigma from 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} in steps of 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} . Figure 3 displays these tests at the base model and at iterations 100 and 500 in the training run, with box-and-whisker plots displayed at each perturbation magnitude. With the base model, the mean reward is largely constant, but its variation increases approximately linearly as perturbation size increases. By iteration 100, perturbation magnitude has a significant, consistent, negative effect on the reward. By iteration 500, this effect is even more consistent and pronounced. In Sudoku in particular, the rewards at magnitude matching the σ \sigma used for training (1e-3) are multiple standard deviations below those of the parent model. Therefore, the perturbation reward distribution strongly depends on the perturbation size ( σ \sigma ). Small σ \sigma ’s produce valid offspring for model improvement, whereas large σ \sigma nearly guarantees that no better models will be produced. If large σ \sigma values in the range where the paradox occurs (e.g. σ = 10 − 3 \sigma=10^{-3} ) lead to worse performance, why not use σ \sigma in the range of ( 1.0 × 10 − 4 , 2.5 × 10 − 4 ) (1.0\times 10^{-4},2.5\times 10^{-4}) where improvement is possible? Indeed, in Figure 3 , when σ \sigma is small enough, the distribution sometimes exceeds parent performance, suggesting that opportunities for improvement exist. However, when σ \sigma is set to these values, ES progress is significantly less, as is tested and shown in Figure 4 . The improvements are lost in the noise, as discussed in detail in Section 5 . However, even though large σ \sigma values result in degraded performance, it turns out they can be used to identify good directions reliably, as discussed in the next section. Even though the smaller perturbation magnitudes produce better candidates, the larger perturbations produce better directions and thus a better overall training run. 4 How Are Good Directions Identified? Section 3 leads to the question: When all models perform worse than the current model, does their relative performance still indicate which directions are more promising? Although it is not possible to directly measure the reward gradient for model checkpoints, it is possible to evaluate the relative performance of perturbations across magnitudes where improving directions do and do not occur. If significant correlations are seen across magnitudes, regardless of performance, then relative performance is indicative of good directions regardless of all perturbation offspring performing worse than the parent. To test this hypothesis, the checkpoints from Sudoku and Countdown runs were again used. The set of 300 perturbation directions was evaluated on each task’s respective 800-problem dataset at magnitudes corresponding to σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} and σ \sigma from 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} in steps of 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} . A correlation matrix was then constructed between the relative rewards of perturbations at these magnitudes. If the perturbation rewards at large σ \sigma contain a signal, then they should correlate with the rewards of the same perturbations at small σ \sigma . From Figure 5 we can see indeed, the rewards are significantly correlated between large and small perturbations, even when the rewards of large perturbations are significantly lower than those of the small perturbations. While greater magnitude differences reduce the measured correlation, the correlations remain positive in most cases. These correlations likely emerge due to a special property of ES with isotropic Gaussian noise in high-dimensional settings. This noise occupies a thin shell in what has been referred to as a “soap bubble” effect ( Huszár, 2017 ) . In a high-dimensional space, all perturbations are nearly identical in norm, effectively canceling out any isotropic curvature in the reward landscape, while leaving differences in relative performance due to the gradient. In other words, the magnitude of noise is identical in all directions, and thus, relative performance allows a signal to still emerge. One way to take advantage of the good directions at large σ \sigma would be to simply follow the best perturbation, instead of performing the aggregation through a weighted sum. To evaluate this ablation, a second test was implemented. The perturbation rewards were sampled on the standard (large) σ \sigma (1e-3), the best of them identified, and the perturbation was scaled down to the size of an average ES update (i.e. a small σ \sigma ). A 500-iteration training run was then run with this process. The training curves along with the fraction of perturbations better than the parent are displayed in Figure 6 . While this best-of-N selection allows making progress, it is still outperformed by the actual ES update. This result suggests that an additional mechanism of aggregation contributes further to the ES performance, as will be discussed next. Sections 3 and 4 demonstrated that model performance decreases with increasing perturbation; however, even when all offspring are worse than the parent, good search directions can be identified among them. This section demonstrates how the ES aggregation mechanism adds value. The insights are drawn from an analytical model of the ES update in a reward landscape with observation noise and quadratic loss. In this model, the ES update can be decomposed into a signal component along the gradient and a noise component orthogonal to it. The model shows that, in expectation, the ES update moves a fixed distance in the direction of the signal, while reducing the magnitude of the noise component via aggregation of offspring. The mean and variance of the ES update in this model were derived independently by ( Hoy et al., 2026 ) , along with a similar decomposition of signal and noise of the update, which they use to estimate parameter drift over training runs. A realistic observation noise term is then introduced, and the model is extended to include curvature. In the end, the optimal perturbation magnitude is determined in the model, showing that it results in likely improvements. Therefore, the paradox is a byproduct of a highly effective ES run. 6 Discussion and Future Work The ES paradox emerged as an unexpected anomaly in population-based search in large spaces. Such methods are presumed to work by creating offspring that are better than parents, yet in many cases ES is able to consistently improve even when this is not true. Understanding the mechanisms behind this paradox led to a new way of thinking about search in high-dimensional spaces: instead of an anomaly, the paradox is a side effect of a principled interaction of noise and curvature in such spaces. This mechanism is different from gradient descent, simulated annealing, and other evolutionary computation, so much so that it can be seen as a paradigm shift in the sense of Kuhn (1970) : an anomaly becomes a fundamental principle in the new way of seeing things. As a result, old assumptions need to be re-evaluated, and new opportunities arise for progress. For instance: Small Population Performance of ES: One of the most dramatic features of the new line of ES work in LLM fine-tuning has been the significantly smaller population size. Previously, it had been assumed that ES had fundamental scaling limitations with respect to high-dimensional spaces ( Jamieson et al., 2012 ) , yet within fine-tuning, it has been competitive with, and often even outperforming, gradient-based reinforcement learning methods. This work now sheds some light on this phenomenon, demonstrating that once the noise component of the ES update is small enough to avoid incurring a significant cost from curvature, the update is able to achieve the maximum improvement in reward - even if the noise component is orders of magnitude larger than the signal component. The surprising Robustness of LLMs to Noise in Parameter Space: From the update reward improvement estimate results in Figure 8 , per step update is seen to plateau at approximately a population size of 30. Future work may look at how to identify these properties during a run, or whether estimation of said optimums is too noisy to do online, but may be aggregated across fine-tuning runs.
